messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 69
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fast Food Worker
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 76

She is sixty-nine, a married Middle Eastern woman who has spent years working the early shift at a fast food restaurant, where she takes pride in being reliable, quick with her hands, and kind to customers even when her feet ache. Before the stalking began, her life is narrow but steady: home, work, the grocery store, the mosque on weekends, calls with relatives overseas. She likes routine. She finds comfort in knowing which bus arrives at what time, which manager will be on shift, how many biscuits to put in the oven before the breakfast rush. She has lived long enough with uncertainty in other parts of life that ordinary predictability feels precious.

The first time she notices the man, she tells herself it is nothing. He is standing across the street from the restaurant near the end of her shift, not eating, not waiting for anyone she can see, just watching. When she leaves to catch the bus, he is still there. A few days later she sees him again, this time outside the corner store near her apartment. He smiles at her in a way that makes her stomach tighten. She lowers her eyes and keeps walking. She is a woman who has learned over decades to avoid trouble by not feeding it.

But he begins to appear everywhere. Outside the restaurant before dawn. At the bus stop after work. In the parking lot when her husband drives her to buy groceries. Once, she looks up from wiping trays in the dining area and sees him through the window, standing under the restaurant sign in the rain. He does not come in. He only watches. After that, she starts checking the glass every few minutes while pretending to clean.

At first she says little at home because she does not want to alarm her husband, who has his own health problems. She tells herself the man will lose interest. Instead, the behavior becomes bolder. He follows her partway home on foot. He calls out comments about her clothes, her smile, how he knows when she gets off work. One afternoon he steps too close at the bus stop and asks why she acts as if she is too good to speak to him. She can smell cigarettes on him. Her body goes cold. She does not remember the bus ride after that; only that when she gets home her hands shake so badly she spills tea across the table.

From then on, fear enters every part of the day. She stops taking the same route home, then realizes he seems to find her anyway. She begins asking coworkers to walk her out after her shift, embarrassed by how old and foolish she feels needing protection. At work she loses track of orders and startles whenever the entrance chime sounds. If a man lingers at the counter, her chest pounds and she cannot breathe deeply enough. She smiles automatically at customers while inside she is scanning faces, windows, doors, reflections on the soda machine. Her manager notices she is slower, more distracted. She says she has not been sleeping.

At night she lies awake listening for sounds in the hallway outside her apartment. Every scrape of shoes, every car door slamming below, feels like a warning. When she does sleep, she wakes drenched in sweat, heart racing, certain for a few seconds that he is in the room. She begins keeping the curtains closed even during the day. She jumps when the phone rings. She asks her husband to check the lock twice, then gets up and checks it herself. Sometimes she stands at the peephole for long stretches, barely breathing.

Eventually her family learns more of what is happening because she cannot contain it anymore. She cries unexpectedly while chopping parsley for dinner. She snaps at her husband when he asks a simple question. She avoids the mosque and declines visits with friends because she is ashamed and because leaving home feels dangerous. Her world shrinks to work and apartment, and even work no longer feels safe. The smell of frying oil, once just part of the job, now mixes in her memory with fear. She watches every car in the lot before stepping outside. If she sees someone in a dark jacket resembling his, her knees weaken.

The stalking persists long enough that she stops expecting it to end. What frightens her most is not only the man himself but the feeling that her own mind has changed. She used to be patient, practical, steady. Now she is exhausted and on edge, forgetting conversations, misplacing her keys, flinching when her husband enters the kitchen behind her. She knows some of her reactions are larger than the moment in front of her, but knowing this does not stop them. Her body reacts before thought arrives.

In the present, she speaks about the stalking in a low, controlled voice, as if too much emotion might make it all happen again. She still works, though each shift costs her. She leaves by different exits when she can. She studies strangers’ faces without meaning to. She sits with her back to walls in public places and asks her husband to wait for her at the bus stop if he is able. She misses the version of herself who could move through the city without calculation. What stays with her is the constant sense of being watched, as though the danger has lodged inside her and now travels with her wherever she goes.
